title: Formal proof-style derivation 89: Systems & LTI Properties — worked from first principles (parameter set 89)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. Equality for all inputs proves the property; a single counterexample disproves it, which is why each derivation ends with an explicit verdict and the boundary case that would change it.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 89)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: T{a x1 + b x2} = a T{x1} + b T{x2} ; delayed input must give delayed output. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 89 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Formal proof-style derivation 89: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 89)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. title: Formal proof-style derivation 89: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 89)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. title: Theoretical derivation 90: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 90)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Communication channels are governed by two complementary laws. Shannon's capacity, built from bandwidth and SNR, is an upper bound no coding can exceed in noise; Nyquist's formula turns a chosen rate into required signal levels on a noiseless channel. title: Theoretical derivation 93: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 93)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. title: Formal proof-style derivation 98: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 98)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. Derivations here compute coefficients from the integral definition, verify power in both domains, and interpret magnitude and phase spectra as instructions for what a filter will do.

title: Numerical derivation 106: Elementary Signals & Operations — worked from first principles (parameter set 106)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Elementary signals are the atoms of the subject. The impulse extracts values through sifting, the step accumulates impulse area, the ramp accumulates the step, and exponentials rotate and scale through Euler's identity. Every complicated waveform in later modules is assembled from shifted, folded and scaled copies of these atoms, so each derivation here isolates one operation, performs it symbolically first, and only then substitutes numbers, keeping sign and shift errors visible rather than hiding them inside arithmetic.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 106)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: integral x(t) delta(t-t0) dt = x(t0) ; u(t) = integral_{-inf}^{t} delta ; e^{jwt} = cos wt + j sin wt. title: Formal proof-style derivation 107: DT Fourier, DFT & Sampling — worked from first principles (parameter set 107)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Discrete-time spectra are periodic with period 2 pi, finite data produce the DFT's N bins, and sampling replicates spectra every fs so that overlap becomes aliasing. The derivations in this module pass carefully between DFS, DTFT and DFT instead of conflating them, evaluate small DFTs directly from the definition sum, and treat the sampling theorem as a geometric statement about spectral copies: recovery is possible exactly when the copies do not overlap, and the anti-alias filter is what enforces that precondition.

A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. Equality for all inputs proves the property; a single counterexample disproves it, which is why each derivation ends with an explicit verdict and the boundary case that would change it.

title: Numerical derivation 109: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 109)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. title: Numerical derivation 109: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 109)

The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. title: Formal proof-style derivation 110: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 110)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION

title: Formal proof-style derivation 113: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 113)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. Each worked entry evaluates the defining sum directly, then re-derives the same answer through a property shortcut, because agreement between the two routes is the strongest available check.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 113)

The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. title: Theoretical derivation 120: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 120)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. title: Formal proof-style derivation 122: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 122)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. title: Theoretical derivation 123: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 123)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. title: Numerical derivation 130: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 130)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION

title: Numerical derivation 133: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 133)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION

title: Formal proof-style derivation 137: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 137)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 137)

title: Theoretical derivation 138: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 138)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. title: Theoretical derivation 144: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 144)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. Derivations here compute coefficients from the integral definition, verify power in both domains, and interpret magnitude and phase spectra as instructions for what a filter will do.

Discrete-time spectra are periodic with period 2 pi, finite data produce the DFT's N bins, and sampling replicates spectra every fs so that overlap becomes aliasing. title: Theoretical derivation 150: Systems & LTI Properties — worked from first principles (parameter set 150)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. title: Theoretical derivation 153: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 153)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. title: Numerical derivation 154: Modulation & Transmission — worked from first principles (parameter set 154)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Modulation moves information onto a carrier by varying amplitude, frequency or phase, and digital keying quantises that variation into constellation points. The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. title: Formal proof-style derivation 158: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 158)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. title: Numerical derivation 160: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 160)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION

title: Numerical derivation 166: Elementary Signals & Operations — worked from first principles (parameter set 166)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Elementary signals are the atoms of the subject. The impulse extracts values through sifting, the step accumulates impulse area, the ramp accumulates the step, and exponentials rotate and scale through Euler's identity. Every complicated waveform in later modules is assembled from shifted, folded and scaled copies of these atoms, so each derivation here isolates one operation, performs it symbolically first, and only then substitutes numbers, keeping sign and shift errors visible rather than hiding them inside arithmetic.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 166)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: integral x(t) delta(t-t0) dt = x(t0) ; u(t) = integral_{-inf}^{t} delta ; e^{jwt} = cos wt + j sin wt. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Discrete-time spectra are periodic with period 2 pi, finite data produce the DFT's N bins, and sampling replicates spectra every fs so that overlap becomes aliasing. The derivations in this module pass carefully between DFS, DTFT and DFT instead of conflating them, evaluate small DFTs directly from the definition sum, and treat the sampling theorem as a geometric statement about spectral copies: recovery is possible exactly when the copies do not overlap, and the anti-alias filter is what enforces that precondition.

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. Equality for all inputs proves the property; a single counterexample disproves it, which is why each derivation ends with an explicit verdict and the boundary case that would change it.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 169)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: T{a x1 + b x2} = a T{x1} + b T{x2} ; delayed input must give delayed output. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 169 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Numerical derivation 169: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 169)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. title: Numerical derivation 169: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 169)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. CONCEPT AND INTUITION

For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. title: Formal proof-style derivation 170: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 170)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Communication channels are governed by two complementary laws. Shannon's capacity, built from bandwidth and SNR, is an upper bound no coding can exceed in noise; Nyquist's formula turns a chosen rate into required signal levels on a noiseless channel. title: Formal proof-style derivation 173: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 173)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. Each worked entry evaluates the defining sum directly, then re-derives the same answer through a property shortcut, because agreement between the two routes is the strongest available check.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 173)

title: Theoretical derivation 174: Modulation & Transmission — worked from first principles (parameter set 174)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Modulation moves information onto a carrier by varying amplitude, frequency or phase, and digital keying quantises that variation into constellation points. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. The derivations here build (A, B, C, D) from differential or difference equations, solve through (sI minus A) inverse or A-to-the-n evolution, and read stability from eigenvalues of A, closing the loop with Modules 5 and 6 because H(s) equals C (sI minus A) inverse B plus D and the eigenvalues are exactly the system poles.
